texts: At an Italian café counter, ask politely whether the other speaks Italian.
You ask someone to repeat what they said.
A polite opener before the conversation continues in Italian.
At the cafe counter, you politely ask whether Italian is spoken here.

Salve is a polite, time-neutral hello in Italian — it works any time of day, so you do not have to choose between "buongiorno" (morning) and "buonasera" (afternoon/evening). Safe with strangers, shopkeepers, and service staff.
Morning light in a cafe, an open counter, and a calm first greeting in Italian.
Mid-exchange, politely ask the other to repeat what they said.
On the street, you ask for the station.
Excuse me, could you repeat that?
A polite request to hear what was just said one more time.
Excuse me, could you repeat that?
Mid-conversation, you raise your hand briefly and politely ask for a repeat.

Scusi is the formal Lei version of "excuse me" and opens any correction, repeat-request, or small pause in conversation at A1. Note: "scusa" is the casual tu form — use "scusi" with strangers and service staff.
Soft cafe light, a brief pause at the counter, a calm repeat-request.
On the street, ask politely where the station is.
At the counter, you order a coffee.
Excuse me, where is the station?
A short, polite question pointing to a clear destination in town.
Excuse me, where is the station?
On the sidewalk, you stop someone briefly and politely ask for the station.
Dove is the core where-word at A1. Before a vowel it elides to "dov'è" (dove + è) — one of the small Italian habits worth catching early. Use "dov'è" for singular things, "dove sono" for plural.
A bright morning street, a station sign in the distance, an open gesture.
At an Italian café counter, order a coffee politely with "vorrei".
In a shop, you ask the price.
A polite order at the counter, using the Italian conditional as a gentle wish.
At the counter the order sounds short, calm, and friendly with the classic "vorrei".
Caffè is the counter word in any Italian bar. In Italy "un caffè" means an espresso — not a big mug of filter coffee. Always write the grave accent: caffè, never caffe. Masculine: il caffè.
An espresso cup on the counter, warm morning light, a calm order.
In a small shop, ask the price of an item.
At the station, you ask about the departure time.
A direct, polite price question about the item in front of you.
In a small shop, you hold the item and ask the price.

Quanto opens any price or quantity question at A1. Before a vowel it often elides to "quant'è" (quanto + è). It also agrees with what you are counting: quanti caffè (masc. plural), quante volte (fem. plural).
A small shop, an item on the counter, a clear price question.
At a station info desk, ask when the train leaves.
At the pharmacy or info desk, you ask for help.
What time does the train leave?
A clear question about the departure time at the station.
What time does the train leave?
At the station info desk, you ask about the departure time.

Treno is the core travel word for Italy at A1. Masculine (il treno) and opens the whole station vocabulary — from "binario" (platform) to "biglietto" (ticket). Italian uses "parte" (leaves) where English uses "departs".
A bright station hall, a departure board in the background, a calm question at the desk.
At a pharmacy or info desk, ask for help politely.
In small talk, you say something nice about the place.
A short, polite request for help without naming the problem yet.
At the pharmacy, you walk calmly to the counter and briefly say that you need help.

Aiuto is the direct help-word at A1 and works in pharmacies, stations, and at any counter. Italian builds "I need" as "ho bisogno di" (literally "I have need of") — the "di" is required, not optional. Three syllables: a-iu-to.
A calm pharmacy counter, clear light, a brief help-request without drama.
Inside a café, make a short positive remark about the place.
While planning, you confirm the meeting for tomorrow.
A short, warm small-talk line about the venue or room you are in.
I like it (literally: it pleases me)
In the cafe, you turn briefly to the other person and say something nice about the place.

Posto is the warm, neutral word for any place, table, or seat at A1 — safer than the more bookish "luogo". Masculine (il posto). Note: "mi piace" is built backwards from English — Italian literally says "it pleases me", so the thing liked is the grammatical subject.
Inside a cafe, warm light, a brief contented glance.
At the end of an encounter, confirm a plan for tomorrow at seven.
You close the scene with thanks and a goodbye.
A short confirmation of a plan with day, time, and a friendly tag.
At the end of the encounter, you casually confirm the plan for tomorrow.

Perfetto is the friendly, light way to agree at A1 — Italians use it on its own as a full reply where English would say "great" or "sounds good". Note: "alle sette" uses Italian's articulated preposition (a + le = alle, "at the") before plural hours.
Late afternoon, a quick handshake or nod, a calm confirmation.
Close the scene with thanks and a polite goodbye.
A warm close with clear thanks and a friendly, polite goodbye.
As you leave, you turn briefly and close the scene warmly and politely.

Arrivederci closes any service scene politely at A1 and is the formal Lei version of "ciao". Literally "to the seeing each other again" — that "a rivederci" shape is what gives the word its warm farewell sound. Use "ciao" only with friends and family.
A door in the background, warm light, a quick thanks on the way out.
Mid-exchange, admit you do not understand and ask for help.
You ask someone to write something down.
Excuse me, I don't understand. Could you help me?
A calm, polite opener: briefly admit something is unclear and ask for help.
Excuse me, I don't understand. Could you help me?
Mid-conversation, you calmly admit you didn't catch something and open the request for help.

Capisco is the core 'I understand' verb at A1 in the first person, and it opens any clarification politely. Negate it simply by putting 'non' in front: non capisco. The subject pronoun 'io' is hidden in the ending.
A counter, a calm gesture, a brief honest request for help.
Ask politely that the information be written down.
You ask someone to show a location on the map.
Could you write it down, please?
A short, polite request to have important information written down.
Could you write it down, please?
At the desk, you hand over a pen or note and ask for something important to be written down.

Scrivere is the A1 verb for any write-request and takes Italian's small endings naturally: scriverlo = 'to write it', scrivermi = 'to write to me'. The pronoun attaches right onto the end of the infinitive.
A notepad on the counter, pen ready, a calm helpful gesture.
Ask someone to show a location on a map or phone.
You ask which of two visible options it should be.
Could you show it to me on the map?
A concrete request to point to a place on a map (or phone).
Could you show it to me
Could you show it to me on the map?
At a counter or on the sidewalk, you hold up the map and ask for a concrete gesture.

Mappa is the street/city map at A1 — the one in your hand or on your phone. Feminine: la mappa. 'Sulla' is the articulated preposition su + la ('on the'). Italian uses 'cartella' for what English calls a 'folder', not 'mappa'.
A street map on the counter, a finger tracing a line, a calm question.
At a counter, ask which of two visible items is meant.
You ask whether something is still in stock.
A short choice question between two visible options.
In front of two small pastries, you briefly point to both and ask the choice question.
Questo is the near demonstrative at A1 and agrees with what it points to: questo caffè (m.s.), questa mela (f.s.), questi panini (m.pl.), queste cose (f.pl.). The far counterpart is 'quello'.
Two small items side by side, a finger pointing first to one, then to the other.
In a small shop, ask whether an item is available.
At the till, you ask if you can pay by card.
A short, polite question about whether a visible item is in stock.
In the small shop, you point briefly to something and ask if it's still in stock.

Disponibile covers both goods ('in stock') and people ('free / has time') at A1 — Italians use it where English speakers might reach for a literal 'do you have...?'. Same form for masculine and feminine singular: il caffè è disponibile, la mela è disponibile.
A shop counter, an item in focus, a calm availability question.
At the till, ask whether you can pay by card.
You ask for the receipt and a bag.
The standard polite question at the counter about whether card payment is possible.
At the till, you briefly hold up the card and ask the standard payment question.
Carta means both 'bank card' and 'paper' in Italian — context decides which. False-friend note for English speakers: a restaurant menu in Italian is 'il menù', not 'la carta'. Feminine: la carta.
A card reader up close, a card in hand, a calm payment gesture.
At the till, ask for the receipt and a bag.
At reception, you give your reservation name.
The receipt and a bag, please.
Two short requests at the close of the sale: take the receipt and add a bag.
The receipt and a bag, please.
At the till, you take the bag and at the same time ask for the receipt.

Scontrino is the standard Italian till-receipt word at A1 — shorter and more everyday than 'ricevuta' (which sounds more like a formal/official receipt). Because it starts with s+consonant, it takes the masculine article 'lo', not 'il': lo scontrino.
A till close-up, a receipt printing out, a bag at the counter.
At a service counter, announce an existing reservation.
The short, clear opener at a restaurant host stand or service desk when a spot is reserved.
At the restaurant host stand, you open the scene briefly and confidently with the reservation cue.

Prenotazione covers any reservation at A1 — restaurant, hotel, hairdresser, doctor. The verb is 'prenotare'. Feminine: la prenotazione. No false-friend trap — it maps one-to-one to English 'reservation'.
A host stand, a small list on the counter, a calm arrival.
Confirm an item or place is the correct one before committing.
You ask for a brief moment.
A short, friendly double-check before you take something or commit.
Before you board or take it, you hold the object up briefly and ask a friendly check question.

Giusto is the warm confirmation word at A1: 'right', 'correct', 'that fits'. Italians often answer with just 'Giusto!' on its own — short and relaxed. The adjective agrees: giusto, giusta, giusti, giuste.
An object in hand, a brief glance up, a friendly check.
Ask someone to wait briefly while you handle a small task.
A calm, polite request for a short pause while you handle something.
Mid-payment you briefly look for the card or the word and politely ask for a moment.
Momento is the universal mini-pause request in Italian service contexts at A1. The synonym 'un attimo' is just as A1 — often even shorter and softer. Masculine: il momento.
A wallet half open, a brief glance down, a calm micro-pause.

On the sidewalk, ask whether to turn right or left.
On the sidewalk, you ask how far the destination is.
A short direction question to a passerby while navigating.
At an intersection, you briefly stop someone and check whether you go right or left.

Destra is the A1 word for 'right' and always pairs with 'sinistra' (left) — the two words anchor every Italian direction-giving exchange. Italian uses 'a destra / a sinistra' (with preposition 'a'), where English just says 'right / left'.
An intersection in the morning, a quick gesture in both directions, a calm check.
Directions and getting around in Italian
On the sidewalk, ask how far the destination is.
In front of the shop, you ask if it is open now.
A short question about how far the destination is from here.
Mid-sidewalk, you check briefly how far the destination still is.

Lontano is the short A1 word for any distance question and pairs with 'vicino' (near). Italian asks 'È lontano?' directly — shorter and simpler than English 'How far is it?'. The adjective agrees: lontano, lontana, lontani, lontane.
A morning sidewalk, a glance into the distance, a calm clarifying gesture.
Directions and getting around in Italian
In front of a shop, ask whether it is open.
At the bus stop, you ask for the right line.
A short question before stepping in: is the place open right now?
In front of a small shop, you glance briefly at the door and check whether it is open.

Aperto is the A1 state-word before any shop visit and pairs with 'chiuso' (closed). Italian uses 'è aperto' (it is open) where English also uses 'is open' — adjective with the copula, not a verb. Agrees: aperto, aperta, aperti, aperte.
A shop door with an open sign, soft morning light, a calm glance at it.
Directions and getting around in Italian
At a bus stop, ask which bus goes downtown.
On the moving bus, you double-check about the next stop.
A clear route question at the stop: which bus fits the destination?
At the bus stop, you calmly ask someone for the right bus into town.

Autobus is the standard Italian word for 'bus'. Masculine, but unusually it does not change in the plural: l'autobus / gli autobus. Spoken Italian often shortens it to just 'bus'. Note: 'in centro' = 'downtown / in the city center' uses 'in' without an article.
A bus stop with a route sign, a quick question toward a waiting passenger.
Directions and getting around in Italian
On a moving bus, confirm whether the next stop is yours.
At the ticket window, you buy a ticket.
Excuse me, is this the next stop?
A short check on a moving bus or tram before getting off.
Excuse me, is this the next stop?
On the moving bus, you turn briefly to the person next to you and check that the next stop is yours.

Fermata is the A1 word for any bus or tram stop. Feminine: la fermata, plural le fermate. It comes from 'fermare' (to stop) — the connection to stopping makes it easy to remember. Different from 'stazione' (train station).
A window on a moving bus, the next-stop display lighting up, a calm double-check.
Directions and getting around in Italian
At a ticket window, buy a simple ticket.
Outside the museum, you ask about the closing time.
The short standard request at the ticket window or machine.
At the ticket window, the order sounds short, calm, and clear.

Biglietto is the A1 word for any ticket — train, bus, tram, museum. Masculine: il biglietto. 'Andata' = one-way, 'andata e ritorno' = round-trip. Note: Italian 'biglietto' looks like English 'billet' (a small note) but always means a transit/admission ticket here.
A ticket-window close-up, a ticket sliding across the counter, a calm payment.
Directions and getting around in Italian
Outside a museum, ask the closing time.
You ask whether the corner is the turning point.
A question about closing time, to fit the visit in.
Outside the museum, you briefly check when it closes before going in.

Chiude is the 3rd-person form of 'chiudere' (to close) and pairs with 'apre' (opens). Italian asks 'A che ora chiude?' ('at what hour does it close?') — structurally simpler than English's 'What time does it close?'
A museum sign with opening hours, late afternoon, a calm glance at the clock.
Directions and getting around in Italian
On the sidewalk, ask whether to turn at the corner.
You choose between walking and taking a taxi.
Do I turn at the corner?
A concrete sidewalk question about whether the corner is the turning point.
Do I turn at the corner?
At a street corner, you point briefly and ask whether this is the turning point.

Angolo is the A1 word for any corner — street, room, geometric. Masculine: l'angolo. The article elides before the vowel: l'angolo (the corner), all'angolo (at the corner, from a + l'angolo). Italian uses elision wherever the article meets a vowel.
A street corner with cobblestones, soft morning light, a finger pointing to the turn.
Directions and getting around in Italian
On the sidewalk, choose between walking and a taxi.
You ask someone on the street for help.
A casual choice question at the end of the sidewalk or before a long walk.
At the end of the sidewalk, you turn briefly to your companion and decide how to go on.
feet (in the phrase "a piedi" = on foot)

Piedi is the plural of 'piede' (foot) and forms the set phrase 'a piedi' (on foot) — one of the most common Italian transport phrases. Italian uses 'a piedi' (on foot) but 'in taxi / in autobus' (by taxi / by bus) — different prepositions for human-powered vs. vehicle transport.
The end of the sidewalk in the evening, a taxi waiting at the curb, a calm decision gesture.
Directions and getting around in Italian
You got off late and ask for help recovering.
Where is my stop? Could you help me?
A calm request for help after the stop has gone past.
Where is my stop? Could you help me?
You get off late, turn calmly, and ask someone on the sidewalk for help.
Fermata is the practical word for a bus or tram stop.
A sidewalk past a bus stop, the bus moving on in the background, a calm gesture for help.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
At the restaurant entrance, ask for a table.
At the table, you ask for the menu.
The short, polite opener at the restaurant entrance with the headcount.
At the restaurant host stand, you give the headcount in a single calm sentence.

Tavolo is the core restaurant word at A1, paired with 'per due / per tre / per quattro' to open any reservation request. Masculine: il tavolo. Plural: i tavoli (regular). Italian uses 'per' (for) plus the number — no 'people' word needed.
A restaurant host stand in the evening, a small table in the background, a brief greeting.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
At the table, ask for the menu.
You order a tea at the table.
The short request for the menu at the table or counter.
Seated at the table, you signal the server for the menu.

Menù is the Italian word for the food menu — for English speakers, do not reach for 'la carta' (that means the wine list or playing cards in Italian, not the food menu). Always write the grave accent: menù, never menu. Masculine: il menù.
A restaurant table, the menu sliding into frame, a calm gesture.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
At a table, order a tea politely with "vorrei".
A polite tea order using the Italian conditional "vorrei".
Seated at the table, you calmly order a tea with the polite conditional phrase.

Tè carries the grave accent to distinguish it from 'te' (you, yourself) — one of the few but important Italian spelling traps at A1. Note: 'caldo' here means 'hot' (drinks); it does NOT mean 'cold' as the English-looking spelling might suggest.
A cup of tea on the table, warm steam, a calm order gesture.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
At a counter or table, specify "no sugar" politely.
At the bakery, you check freshness.
A short preference for the drink — no sugar.
At the counter or table, you briefly state the preference as the drink is prepared.

Senza is the A1 preposition for any 'without' and pairs with 'con' (with). Short and precise — no article needed: senza zucchero, senza latte, senza problema. Italian 'latte' means 'milk' (not 'latte coffee') — false-friend for English speakers.
A sugar bowl on the counter, a brief hand gesture declining, a calm spoken moment.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
At a bakery counter, ask whether the bread is fresh.
You wrap up the order politely.
A short quality question about bread, fruit, or other food at the counter.
At the bakery counter, you briefly point to a piece of bread and check the freshness.

Fresco agrees with the noun it describes at A1: il pane è fresco (m.s.), la frutta è fresca (f.s.), i panini sono freschi (m.pl.), le mele sono fresche (f.pl.). One of the first Italian adjective-agreement drills.
A bakery counter with bread, a brief gesture toward the choice, a soft flour-dusted glow.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
Respond to "anything else?" with a polite close.
You ask for the order to be takeaway.
The friendly closing reply to the service question "Anything else?".
At the counter, you close the order politely with a brief reply.

Altro is the A1 pronoun for 'anything else / more', and forms the elided phrase 'nient'altro' (niente + altro = nothing else). Italian service staff almost always ask 'Vuole altro?' (Would you like anything else?) — this is the standard closing reply.
A counter close-up after the order, a brief closing gesture, a calm smile.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
At a counter, ask for the order to be takeaway.
After the meal, you give a brief compliment.
The set phrase at the counter for takeaway orders.
At the counter, you give the set takeaway phrase while ordering.

Portare is the A1 all-purpose verb for 'to carry / take'. The fixed phrase 'da portare via' (literally 'to carry away') is Italy's standard 'to go / takeaway' — paired with 'qui' (here / for here) at counters.
A takeaway bag on the counter, a brief handoff gesture, a calm exit.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
After the meal, give a short positive verdict.
Brief small talk with the waiter.
A short, warm compliment after eating or drinking.
At the table after the meal, you turn briefly to the waiter and compliment the food.
Buono agrees with the noun: il caffè è buono, la pasta è buona, i panini sono buoni, and le pizze sono buone.
An empty plate on the table, a satisfied glance, a brief gesture of thanks.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
At a counter, share a short positive comment about the day.
At the end of the meal, you ask for the bill.
A short, easy small-talk remark about today at the counter.
At the counter, you turn casually to the server and share a brief positive comment.

Oggi is the A1 core time word for 'today' and rounds out the trio with 'ieri' (yesterday) and 'domani' (tomorrow). Italian distinguishes 'giorno' (day, as a unit) from 'giornata' (day as a span of experience) — 'che giornata!' = 'what a day!' in feel.
A cafe counter in the morning, sunlight through the window, a brief remark about the day.
At the cafe and restaurant in Italian
At the end of the meal, ask for the bill.
The set closing request at the table for the bill.
At the end of the meal, you briefly raise your hand and ask for the bill.

Conto is the Italian word for the bill at the table at A1. Masculine: il conto. Polysemous: 'conto in banca' = bank account; 'fare i conti' = to settle / do the math. In a restaurant it always means the bill — short and clear: 'il conto'.
A small tray with the bill on the table, quiet evening light, a friendly close.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
Casually apologize to a friend for being late.
You admit the name has slipped your mind.
A short, casual apology to a friend when you're late.
You walk in a bit late and casually apologize to a friend.

Tardi is the A1 adverb for 'late' (paired with 'presto' = early). Related noun 'ritardo' is separate: 'in ritardo' = running late. Note: 'scusa' (casual tu) is what friends use; 'scusi' (formal Lei) is for strangers and service staff.
A doorway in the foreground, a friend waiting at the table, a brief apology gesture.

Admit you forgot a name or detail.
You ask the other person's name.
I do not remember the name.
An honest, casual admission that you lost track of a detail.
I do not remember the name.
Mid-conversation, you calmly admit the name has slipped your mind.
Ricordo means I remember; non ricordo is the useful present-tense phrase for I do not remember.
A brief thoughtful pause, a hand at the head, an honest glance.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
In a casual setting, ask the other for their name.
You reply warmly after the introduction.
The classic Italian name question among peers.
Casually in conversation, you turn to the other person and ask for their name.

Nome is the first name; surname is 'cognome'. Italian uses a reflexive: 'Come ti chiami?' literally means 'How do you call yourself?' — answer with 'Mi chiamo...' (I'm called...). This is the universal Italian opener with peers.
A casual meeting, open eye contact, a brief introduction gesture.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
Reply warmly after a casual introduction.
You ask where the other is from.
The warm, classic reply after a first introduction.
After the first introduction, you give a warm, brief reply.

Piacere as a noun means 'pleasure' and is used as a short reply at first meetings — a complete answer on its own. Often strengthened with 'mio' ('the pleasure is mine'). Same word also exists as a verb (to please, like 'mi piace') — context disambiguates clearly.
A brief handshake or cheek kiss, a calm greeting moment.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
Casually ask where the other is from.
You check if the other is from around here.
The casual where-are-you-from question when meeting someone.
In conversation, you casually ask where the other person is from.
you come (2nd person sg. of venire)

Vieni is the 2nd-person singular of 'venire' (to come) — one of the first irregular verbs at A1. The standard pair: 'Da dove vieni?' (Where are you from?) → 'Vengo da...' (I come from...). Italian drops the pronoun — 'tu' is hidden in the ending.
A conversation at a table, a map or globe in the background, a brief open question.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
Check whether the other is local.
You ask if the other is free tonight.
A short question about whether the other is local.
In casual conversation, you check if the other person is from the city.
Qui is the A1 spatial 'here' and pairs with 'lì' / 'là' (there). Short and very Italian — works in any location question. The synonym 'qua' is also A1 and interchangeable in most contexts.
A cafe corner, relaxed shoulders, a brief glance out the window.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
Ask whether the other has time tonight.
The direct, casual question about whether someone is free for the evening.
Near the end of the chat, you casually ask about free time for the evening.

Stasera is an A1 fusion of 'questa sera' (this evening), distinct from 'ieri sera' (last night) and 'domani sera' (tomorrow night). Note also: 'libero' agrees with the listener's gender — libero for a man, libera for a woman.
Late afternoon light in the cafe, a casual lean, an open invitation gesture.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
You move the plan to tomorrow.
Shall we meet at the café?
A casual meet-up suggestion — the cafe as Italy's default meeting spot.
Shall we meet at the café?
You make a casual meet-up suggestion by the cafe window.

False-friend trap for English speakers: in Italy, 'il bar' is the everyday daytime coffee place — espresso, pastries, small talk — NOT an evening cocktail bar. For drinks at night, Italians say 'pub' or 'bar' with context. 'Ci vediamo' = 'we'll see each other' (reflexive).
A view of an Italian cafe facade through the window, a brief moment of suggestion.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
You say a casual goodbye until tomorrow.
A gentle postponement of the plan to the next day.
You politely shift the plan to another day.
maybe / I wish (with a wishful tone)

Magari is a key A1 Italian word with two senses: politely tentative ('maybe, probably not') and enthusiastically wishful ('I wish!' / 'if only!'). Tone decides which. Very Italian — no direct English equivalent; closest is 'maybe' for soft-decline, 'I wish' for the enthusiastic sense.
A brief open glance aside, a casual shrug, a calm shift gesture.
Meeting people and making plans in Italian
Close the casual encounter with "see you tomorrow".
Italy's short standard goodbye when you'll see each other again the next day.
At the end of the meet-up, you close with a quick, warm see-you-tomorrow.

Domani is the A1 standard for 'tomorrow' as a day. For 'tomorrow morning' (time of day) Italian uses 'domani mattina'. 'A domani!' (literally 'to tomorrow!') is the short casual goodbye among friends — 'ciao' is the matching informal bye.
A cafe exit in the evening, a brief wave, warm light trailing on the way out.
Pharmacy and small ailments in Italian
At a pharmacy counter, signal you feel unwell and ask for help.
You ask for the nearest pharmacy.
I'm not feeling well. Could you help me?
A calm, polite opener at the pharmacy counter when something is off.
I'm not feeling well. Could you help me?
At the pharmacy counter, you calmly say in one sentence that you're not feeling well.

Bene is the adverb paired with 'stare' (to be / feel) at A1 — don't use 'buono' (adjective, meaning 'good' for things like food). 'Sto bene' / 'Non sto bene' is the core Italian phrase for how you feel. Italian uses 'stare' (not 'essere') for transient feelings.
A pharmacy counter, a small preparatory gesture, a calm honest glance.
Pharmacy and small ailments in Italian
On the sidewalk, ask whether a pharmacy is nearby.
At the pharmacy, you ask for medicine.
A short there-is question on the sidewalk while looking for the nearest pharmacy.
On the sidewalk, you briefly stop a passerby and ask for the nearest pharmacy.

Farmacia is the Italian pharmacy at A1 — look for the green cross sign. Feminine: la farmacia. The 'there-is' phrase 'c'è' is an elision of 'ci + è' — Italy's standard way to ask if something exists nearby. False-friend note: 'farmacia' is pharmacy, NOT 'farm' (which is 'fattoria').
A sidewalk close-up with a green pharmacy cross in the background, a brief searching gesture.
Pharmacy and small ailments in Italian
At a pharmacy counter, ask for medicine in a general way.
You point to where it hurts.
A short, polite request for medicine at the pharmacy counter.
At the pharmacy counter, you ask in one calm sentence for medicine.

Medicina is the Italian word for both 'medicine' (the medication) and 'medicine' (the field of study). At the pharmacy you typically say 'una medicina per...' (a medicine for...) — an A1-safe opener without needing diagnosis vocabulary. Feminine: la medicina.
A pharmacy counter with small boxes in the background, a calm request gesture.
Pharmacy and small ailments in Italian
Point to a body location and say it hurts.
You name your symptom — a headache.
A direct, gesture-paired pain statement — point to the spot.

Acqua starts with a vowel at A1, so it takes the elided forms: l'acqua (not 'la acqua'), un'acqua (not 'una acqua'), and in the phrase d'acqua (not 'di acqua'). One of the most important elision drills in A1 Italian. Feminine noun: la mia acqua.

Medico is the doctor in general; 'dottore' is the personal title ('Dottore, mi può aiutare?'). Italians switch between both flexibly in daily life. Note: this is not emergency vocabulary — for emergencies it's 'pronto soccorso' (A&E / ER). Masculine: il medico.

Allergico agrees with the speaker's gender: men say 'sono allergico', women say 'sono allergica' (plural: allergici / allergiche). The preposition 'a' merges with the article: al latte (to milk), alle noci (to nuts), ai pesci (to fish) — articulated prepositions are everywhere in Italian.

Dormire is the A1 verb for to sleep — a regular -ire verb: dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono. The 'vado a + infinitive' pattern (vado a dormire / vado a mangiare) is Italy's most common construction for stating intent — like English 'I'm going to sleep / eat'.

Serata at A1 is evening as a SPAN of time (several hours); 'sera' is evening as a POINT in time. English doesn't separate these. 'Buona serata' (for the whole evening) is the standard Italian service-context farewell when leaving.
